+
+This document describes the support requirements, software version support, and deprecation policy for Spanner Omni.
+
+## Requirements for Spanner Omni support
+
+To troubleshoot business-critical incidents, do the following before you contact Cloud Customer Care:
+
+- Check that your environment is current and within the published end-of-support timeframes. For more information, see [Version support policy](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner-omni/support#version-support-policy) .
+
+- Collect and share Spanner Omni diagnostics. For more information, see [Connectivity and diagnostics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner-omni/overview#connectivity-development) .
+
+## Version support policy
+
+The following policies govern Spanner Omni software support and deprecation:
+
+- To receive Spanner Omni support, you must sign up for [premium support](https://docs.cloud.google.com/support) .
+
+- Spanner Omni support starts when you purchase a commercial license for the [Commercial edition](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner-omni/editions-overview#commercial-edition) .
+
+- The support period for each subsequent long-term support (LTS) release that you install is one year starting from the release date of that LTS release.
+
+- Google recommends that you install each LTS release within 60 days of its release date.
+
+- Google provides support for each short-term support (STS) release until the date of the next STS or LTS release, whichever comes sooner. The support period for an STS release starts on its release date.

+---
+name: documents/docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cutover-fallback
+uri: https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/cutover-fallback
+title: Configure fallback and cutover
+description: Use fallback and cutover when migrating your database to Spanner to minimize downtime and risk.

+---
+
+Migrations are often time-consuming and complex. It is possible that after data migration and cutover, you might encounter inconsistent performance or issues with the Spanner database.
+
+We recommend configuring fallback from your Spanner database before performing cutover to avoid significant impact if an error occurs during migration. Fallback lets you revert to the source database with minimal downtime.
+
+Reverse replication supports fallback by replicating data written to Spanner back to your source database. If you need to fall back, you can then point your application to the source database and continue serving requests with minimal downtime.
+
+Spanner provides prebuilt reverse replication pipelines that handle this process out of the box, so you don't need to build custom reverse replication tooling. The pipeline automatically does the following:
+
+- Handles changes in data types and schema mappings between Spanner and your source database.
+- Reverses any transformations performed during the forward migration.
+- Routes data to the appropriate destination, taking into account sharding schemes on the source database.
+- Captures changes from Spanner change streams before writing to your source database, ensuring consistency eventually.
+- Manages error handling and retries through dead-letter queues.
+
+## Source-specific guides
+
+Use the following guides for each phase of fallback and cutover:
+
+- MySQL:
+  - [Configure fallback to MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/mysql-configure-fallback) .
+  - [Perform cutover from MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/mysql-perform-cutover) .
+  - [Perform fallback to MySQL](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/mysql-fallback) .

 ## JSON and JSONB queries
 
-You can use a search index to accelerate queries that include *JSON containment* and *key existence* conditions. JSON containment determines if one JSON document is contained within another. Key existence determines if a key exists in the database schema.
+You can use a search index to accelerate queries that include *equality comparisons* , *JSON containment* , and *key existence* conditions:
+
+- **Equality comparisons** determine whether a JSON document or a subpath within a JSON document equals a target value.
+- **JSON containment** determines if one JSON document is contained within another.
+- **Key existence** determines if a key or path exists in a JSON document.
+
+You can express these conditions in each dialect as follows:
 
 - In GoogleSQL:
 
+  - Construct equality predicates using the `=` , `!=` , `<>` , `IN` , and `NOT IN` operators on an indexed `JSON` column or a subpath extracted with the [field access](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/operators#field_access_operator) and [subscript](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/operators#json_subscript_operator) operators. For example, `doc = JSON '{"a": 1}'` , `doc.sub.path[0].key = "value"` , or `doc.status IN ("active", "pending")` . Other [comparison operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/data-types#comparison_and_sorting) such as `<` , `<=` , `>` , and `>=` aren't accelerated by JSON search indexes.
   - Express JSON containment in your schema by using the [`JSON_CONTAINS`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/standard-sql/json_functions#json_contains) function.
   - Construct key existence conditions using the field access, array subscript operators, and `IS NOT NULL` . The field access and array subscript operators describe a JSON document path. `IS NOT NULL` checks for the existence of this path (for example, `doc.sub.path[@index].key IS NOT NULL` ).
 
 - In PostgreSQL:
 
+  - Construct equality predicates using the `=` , `!=` , `<>` , `IN` , and `NOT IN` operators on an indexed `JSONB` column or a subpath extracted with the [`->`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/postgresql/functions-and-operators#jsonb_operators) operator. For example, `doc = '{"a": 1}'::jsonb` , `doc->'sub'->0->'key' = '"value"'::jsonb` , or `doc->'status' IN ('"active"'::jsonb, '"pending"'::jsonb)` . Other comparison operators such as `<` , `<=` , `>` , and `>=` , as well as text extraction predicates that use `->>` , aren't accelerated by JSONB search indexes.
   - Express JSONB containment using the `@>` and `<@` operators. For more information, see [JSONB operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/postgresql/functions-and-operators#jsonb_operators) .
   - Construct key existence conditions using the `?` , `?|` , and `?&` operators. For more information, see [JSONB operators](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/reference/postgresql/functions-and-operators#jsonb_operators) .

-
-To fix the following issues, always use property value conversions when using a property inside a query expression.

-#### Property values comparison without conversion
-
-**Issue**
-
-```
-No matching signature for operator = for argument types: JSON, STRING
-```
-
-**Possible cause**
-
-The query doesn't properly convert property values. For example, the `name` property is not converted to `STRING` type in comparison:
-
-```

-MATCH (p:Person)
-WHERE p.name = "Alex"
-RETURN p.id;
-```
-
-**Recommended solution**
-
-To fix this issue, use a value conversion before comparison.
-
-```
-GRAPH FinGraph
-MATCH (p:Person)
-WHERE STRING(p.name) = "Alex"
-RETURN p.id;
-```
-
-This returns results similar to the following:
-
-```
-+------+
-| id   |
-+------+
-| 1    |
-+------+
-```

-
-```
-GRAPH FinGraph
-MATCH (p:Person {name: 'Alex'})
-RETURN p.id;
-```
-
-This returns results similar to the following:
-
-```

-+------+

-+------+
-```

+## Monitor and resolve reverse replication errors
+
+When running reverse replication from Spanner back to MySQL, if your streaming Dataflow job can't write a change event to your MySQL primary database, it classifies the failure into one of two categories and writes the record to a dead-letter queue directory in your Cloud Storage bucket:
+
+- **Retryable errors** : Temporary failures, such as MySQL database lock contention or network connection timeouts. Dataflow writes these events to a `retry/` dead-letter queue directory and automatically retries them within the same pipeline until they succeed or exceed `dlqMaxRetryCount` .
+- **Severe errors** : Permanent failures that cannot be resolved by automatic retries, such as data type conversion errors, syntax errors, or exceptions inside custom transformation JARs. Dataflow writes these events to a `severe/` dead-letter queue directory (for example, `gs://MIGRATION_BUCKET/ENV/SERVICE/reverse/DB_SCHEMA/severe/` ) and increments the custom user counter `severe_error_count` .
+
+Because severe errors cannot be resolved by automatic retries, Dataflow removes those failed events from the active replication stream and saves them in the `severe/` directory. If left unhandled, your rollback MySQL database will be missing those records. Regularly monitor the `severe_error_count` counter and the `severe/` directory during reverse replication so you can resolve and replay failed change events before initiating a rollback.
+
+The Dataflow custom counter `severe_error_count` is a cumulative metric that records the total number of severe errors encountered since the streaming job started. When you replay and resolve failed records by using a DLQ retry job, this counter on your original streaming pipeline doesn't decrement. Therefore, your Cloud Storage severe DLQ directory ( `gs://MIGRATION_BUCKET/ENV/SERVICE/reverse/DB_SCHEMA/severe/` ) is the authoritative source of truth for whether unhandled errors exist.
+

+When failed records appear in your severe DLQ directory, inspect the JSON error files in Cloud Storage, identify the root cause, and resolve the underlying issue.

+
+During live change data capture (CDC) replication from MySQL to Spanner, if your streaming Dataflow job can't write a change event to Spanner, it classifies the failure into one of two error categories and writes the record to a DLQ directory in the `deadLetterQueueDirectory` Cloud Storage bucket:

+

+

+
+  - Data type conversion errors
+  - Unique index violations
+  - Exceptions inside custom transformation JARs
